title: Eisenstein Integers ℤ[ω]: Ring, Norm, and Euclidean Structure (toward x² + 3y²)
description: S2 + S3 ACT for the third open question of zsqrtd-neg-two: extending the parent's x² + 2y² representation theorem to x² + 3y² via the Eisenstein integers ℤ[ω]. The S2 layer (~207 LOC) establishes the algebraic foundation — the concrete structure on (re, im) ∈ ℤ × ℤ representing re + im·ω with ω² + ω + 1 = 0, the full CommRing instance via the Zsqrtd.commRing template, and the algebraic norm N(a + bω) = a² - ab + b² with norm_nonneg/norm_mul/norm_eq_zero_iff/norm_pos_of_ne_zero. The S3 layer (+223 LOC, file now 430 LOC) installs the Euclidean structure: the conjugate conj (a + bω) = (a - b) + (-b)·ω, division by rounding (instDiv via round((x·conj y)/N(y))), the geometric core sq_rounding_error_lt_one (rounding error ≤ 3/4 < 1 via 4(a² - ab + b²) = (2a - b)² + 3b²), the central decreasing-norm inequality norm_mod_lt, and the full EuclideanDomain instance with Euclidean function (norm ·).natAbs. By Mathlib's instance chain this makes Eisenstein automatically a UFD. The splitting argument (-3/p) = (p/3) via quadratic reciprocity and the main representation theorem are deferred to S4-S5.

meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The S2 + S3 ACT deliverables are present: bare ring, norm, Eisenstein conjugate, division by rounding, and the EuclideanDomain instance. The splitting argument via quadratic reciprocity and the main `p = x² + 3y²` theorem will land in S4-S5 follow-up work.

sections.title: Structure and Primitive Instances
sections.summary: `structure Eisenstein` with two integer coordinates `re, im`, the `ofInt` coercion, and primitive instances `Zero, One, Add, Neg, Mul` together with twelve `@[simp] rfl` projection lemmas for `re/im` on these constructions (zero, one, add, neg, mul) plus the integer-coercion lemmas re_ofInt / im_ofInt.
sections.mathContext: The multiplication is derived from `ω² + ω + 1 = 0`: `(a + bω)(c + dω) = ac + (ad + bc)ω + bd · ω² = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc - bd)ω`. The projection lemmas expose the constructor form so that `simp` can fire during the ring-axiom proofs.

sections.title: AddCommGroup, AddGroupWithOne, CommRing
sections.summary: Builds the ring structure ladder via the Mathlib `Zsqrtd.commRing` template: `addCommGroup` with explicit `nsmulRec/zsmulRec` and `add_assoc`-style refinements; `addGroupWithOne` with `natCast := ofInt ∘ Int.ofNat` and `intCast := ofInt`; `commRing` with explicit `npowRec` and the ring axioms. Interleaved are `sub_re` and `sub_im` simp lemmas (derived from `sub_eq_add_neg`).
sections.mathContext: Each axiom is closed by `intros; ext <;> simp <;> ring` — the simp lemmas unfold the projection-component form so that `ring` can normalize the integer arithmetic. This is the exact pattern used in `Mathlib/NumberTheory/Zsqrtd/Basic.lean` around line 164.

sections.title: Norm Definition and Non-Negativity
sections.summary: Defines the Eisenstein norm `N(a + bω) = a² - ab + b²` together with the trivial `norm_zero`, `norm_one` (closed by `simp [norm]`) and the load-bearing `norm_nonneg` lemma. The latter rests on the algebraic identity `4 · N(z) = (2 re - im)² + 3 · im²` proved by `simp only [norm]; ring`, closed by `nlinarith [sq_nonneg (2 * z.re - z.im), sq_nonneg z.im]`.
sections.mathContext: The non-negativity certificate `4 · (a² - ab + b²) = (2a - b)² + 3 b²` is the same `disc(x² - x + 1) = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0` discriminant identity that shows `x² - x + 1 > 0` over ℝ. It establishes that `N` is a positive-definite integral quadratic form of discriminant `-3` — exactly the form whose `SL₂(ℤ)`-equivalence class generates the (trivial) class group of `ℚ(√-3)`.

sections.title: Norm Multiplicativity and Zero Criterion
sections.summary: Establishes the three structural properties of the norm needed downstream: `norm_mul` (multiplicativity `N(xy) = N(x) · N(y)` via `simp only [norm, mul_re, mul_im]; ring`), `norm_eq_zero_iff` (the two-square split — extracting `z.re = z.im = 0` from `(2·re - im)² = im² = 0` using `pow_eq_zero_iff` and `linarith`), and `norm_pos_of_ne_zero` (strict positivity on nonzero elements, derived from `norm_nonneg` + `norm_eq_zero_iff`).
sections.mathContext: Multiplicativity is the algebraic spine of the entire downstream proof: it makes `N : Eisenstein → ℤ` a monoid homomorphism, so that primality in `ℤ` reflects irreducibility in `ℤ[ω]`. The zero criterion `N(z) = 0 ↔ z = 0` is what promotes `ℤ[ω]` to a domain (it forbids zero divisors via the norm map). Strict positivity on nonzero elements is then automatic, and provides the well-founded measure required for the S3 EuclideanDomain instance: any valid quotient/remainder pair `(q, r)` with `0 ≤ N(r) < N(divisor)` terminates the division algorithm.

overview.historicalContext: The theorem `prime p ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⟹ p = a² + 3 b²` was first proved by **Leonhard Euler** in 1763 (*De numeris qui sunt aggregata duorum quadratorum multiplicatorum*) as a generalization of Fermat's two-squares theorem. The cleanest modern proof uses the **Eisenstein integers** `ℤ[ω]`, where `ω = exp(2πi/3)`. The ring `ℤ[ω]` is the ring of integers of `ℚ(√-3)`, a Euclidean domain (and hence PID) under the norm `N(a + bω) = a² - ab + b²`; this allows the splitting argument that `prime p ≡ 1 (mod 3)` is non-irreducible in `ℤ[ω]` and hence equals `N(α)` for some `α`, which converts to `4p = (2a - b)² + 3 b²` and after parity analysis to `p = x² + 3 y²`. **Gauss** (*Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*, 1801) generalized this to all imaginary quadratic forms `a x² + b xy + c y²` with discriminant `b² - 4 ac < 0`. The class-number-one cases `n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163}` (the **Heegner numbers**) admit such direct constructions; for general `n`, **class field theory** (Cox, *Primes of the form x² + n y²*, 1989) is required.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question (zsqrtd-neg-two-oq-03):** Can the parent gallery proof `zsqrtd-neg-two` (which formalizes the `n = 2` case `p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8) ⟹ p = a² + 2 b²`) be replayed for the next class-number-one Heegner numbers `n ∈ {3, 7, 11}`?

**S2 ACT (this file):** Build the algebraic infrastructure layer — the concrete Eisenstein structure, the full `CommRing` instance, the algebraic norm, and the four key norm properties (non-negativity, multiplicativity, the zero criterion, and strict positivity on nonzero elements) — that the subsequent S3-S5 sessions will build on.
overview.text: Infrastructure for the n = 3 Heegner-number case of Fermat's two-squares-style theorem: ℤ[ω] = ℤ[exp(2πi/3)] as a CommRing with multiplicative norm.
overview.proofStrategy: Three layers: (1) a fresh concrete structure on (re, im) ∈ ℤ × ℤ representing re + im·ω, with primitive instances and `@[simp] rfl` projections; (2) the ring-axiom ladder (`AddCommGroup` → `AddGroupWithOne` → `CommRing`) discharged uniformly by `refine ... <;> intros <;> ext <;> simp <;> ring`, exactly matching the Mathlib `Zsqrtd.commRing` template; (3) the norm `N(a + bω) = a² - ab + b²` with non-negativity via `4 N(z) = (2 re - im)² + 3 im² ≥ 0` and multiplicativity via direct `ring` expansion after `simp [mul_re, mul_im]`.
keyInsights: **Why a fresh structure, not `Zsqrtd (-3)`**: `ℤ[√-3]` is **not** the ring of integers of `ℚ(√-3)`. The maximal order is `ℤ[(1 + √-3)/2] = ℤ[ω]`, strictly larger. The parent file `Proofs/ZsqrtdNegTwo.lean` (for `n = 2`) can use `Zsqrtd (-2)` because `ℤ[√-2]` happens to coincide with the maximal order — that coincidence breaks at `n ≥ 3`.

**Why the `Zsqrtd.commRing` template works for Eisenstein**: the multiplication `(a + bω)(c + dω) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc - bd)ω` is polynomial in the coordinates, so `<;> intros <;> ext <;> simp <;> ring` closes every ring axiom uniformly — the same way it closes them for the `√d` case.

**The `4 N(z) = (2 re - im)² + 3 im²` identity**: this is the algebraic non-negativity certificate. It is equivalent to `disc(x² - x + 1) = -3 < 0` and shows that `N` is a positive-definite quadratic form. The same identity drives the rounding-error bound `(1/4)² + 3 · (1/4)² = 1/4 < 1` for the EuclideanDomain instance in S3.

**The norm is multiplicative for free**: because `Eisenstein` is a commutative ring and `norm = self * conjugate` (with `conjugate (a + bω) = a + bω̄ = (a - b) - bω` in our coordinates), multiplicativity follows from associativity + commutativity by `ring`. No analytic argument is needed.

**Heegner numbers explain why this template stops at $n = 11$**: the imaginary quadratic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-n})$ with class number 1 are exactly $n \in \{1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163\}$ (Heegner 1952, Stark 1967, Baker 1966) — only nine values. The proof template `prime $\Rightarrow$ non-irreducible in maximal order $\Rightarrow$ $p = N(\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow$ $p = $ quadratic form' relies on the maximal order being a PID, which by the principal-ideal-domain $\Leftrightarrow$ unique-factorisation $\Leftrightarrow$ class-number-1 chain is equivalent to $h(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-n})) = 1$. The current file unblocks $n = 3$; sessions S6+ extend through $n = 7$ and $n = 11$; beyond that ($n = 19, 43, 67, 163$) requires Gauss's *form class group* and *binary quadratic form composition* machinery (not in Mathlib 2026), and for non-Heegner $n$ requires class field theory (Cox 1989). The threshold $n = 11$ is therefore a structural maximum of this particular elementary proof method, not an arbitrary stopping point.

**The cyclotomic identity $\mathbb{Z}[\omega] = \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_3]$**: this file's ring is simultaneously the maximal order of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$ and the $3$rd cyclotomic ring of integers $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_3] = \mathbb{Z}[X]/\Phi_3(X)$, where $\Phi_3(X) = X^2 + X + 1$ is the $3$rd cyclotomic polynomial. The coincidence is special to $n = 3$ — for the next quadratic Heegner case $n = 7$, the maximal order $\mathbb{Z}[(1 + \sqrt{-7})/2]$ is **not** cyclotomic (the $7$th cyclotomic ring $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_7]$ has degree $6$ over $\mathbb{Z}$, far larger). The unit group reflects this: $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]^\times = \{1, \omega, \omega^2, -1, -\omega, -\omega^2\} \cong \mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ is the group of $6$th roots of unity, while $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-7})/2]^\times = \{\pm 1\}$ is much smaller. This unit-group difference is mechanically relevant in S3: the EuclideanDomain quotient $q$ and remainder $r$ are not unique — any unit factor can be absorbed — and the choice of $6$ units in $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ versus $2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-7})/2]$ changes the rounding-to-lattice algorithm's branching structure.

**Geometric picture: the Eisenstein lattice as a triangular packing**. Under the embedding $\mathbb{Z}[\omega] \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, $a + b\omega \mapsto a + b \cdot e^{2\pi i / 3}$, the ring becomes the **hexagonal close-packed lattice** with fundamental domain a $60^\circ/120^\circ$ rhombus of area $\sqrt{3}/2$. The algebraic norm $N(a + b\omega) = a^2 - ab + b^2$ equals the squared complex modulus $|a + b\omega|^2$ — that is, $N$ measures the *squared distance from the origin* in the lattice. The covering radius of the triangular lattice (the maximum distance from any point of $\mathbb{C}$ to the nearest lattice point) is $1/\sqrt{3}$, so $N(\mathrm{nearest\,error}) \le 1/3 < 1$ — this **is** the rounding bound that makes $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ a Euclidean domain in S3. By contrast, the square lattice $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ has covering radius $1/\sqrt{2}$, giving the (still-sufficient) bound $1/2$; and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$ — the index-$2$ non-maximal sublattice — has covering radius $1$, so its norm-bound is exactly $1$, *just* failing the strict-inequality test. This is the **geometric** reason why $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$ is not Euclidean while $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ is, dual to the algebraic reason (non-maximality). The integer identity $4N \ge 0$ and the geometry (triangular vs square packing) are two views of the same positive-definite quadratic form.
prerequisites: Imaginary quadratic number fields (`ℚ(√d)` for `d < 0` squarefree)

conclusion.summary: S2 ACT delivers the Eisenstein algebraic-infrastructure layer: structure + CommRing + norm with the four structural identities (`norm_zero`, `norm_one`, `norm_nonneg`, `norm_mul`) plus `norm_eq_zero_iff` and `norm_pos_of_ne_zero`. The file is 207 lines, 20 theorems, 2 definitions, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: **S3 unblocked**: the `EuclideanDomain Eisenstein` instance can now be built on top of `CommRing` + `norm_mul`. **S4-S5 unblocked**: the splitting argument `(-3/p) = (p/3)` via QR + `4p = (2a - b)² + 3 b²` parity case-split now has a well-defined target ring to work in. **n = 7, 11 (S6+)**: the same template generalizes to `ℤ[(1 + √-n)/2]` with norm form `a² + ab + ((n+1)/4) b²`.
openQuestions: Build the EuclideanDomain Eisenstein instance via rounding-to-ℤ (S3, ~200 lines): the key step is the rounding-error bound `N(error) ≤ 1/4 < 1`.
Verify or derive `ZMod.exists_sq_eq_neg_three_iff` at Mathlib v4.26.0 (S4, ~30-50 lines): the analog of the parent's `exists_sq_eq_neg_two_iff`.
Prove `sq_add_three_sq_of_prime_one_mod_three` (S5, ~100 lines): the main `p = x² + 3 y²` representation theorem.

Characterise $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]^\times$ (~20 lines): show `IsUnit z ↔ norm z = 1` and then enumerate the six units $\{1, \omega, \omega^2, -1, -\omega, -\omega^2\}$ (concretely: $|re|, |im| \le 1$ with $|re| + |im| \le 2$ and the parity constraint from $a^2 - ab + b^2 = 1$). This is a prerequisite for the EuclideanDomain quot/rem normalisation in S3 — without unit normalisation, `gcd` does not stabilise.

Port to n = 7 and n = 11 (S6+, ~400 lines each): the maximal-order construction `ℤ[(1 + √-n)/2]` with norm form `a² + ab + ((n+1)/4) b²`. Note that the cyclotomic coincidence breaks: $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-7})/2]$ is not $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_7]$, and the unit group collapses to $\{\pm 1\}$.

**Characterise the image of $N$ — the Loeschian numbers** (~80 lines, S7+): prove `loeschian_iff_image_norm : (∃ z : Eisenstein, z.norm = n) ↔ (∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → q % 3 = 2 → Even (n.factorization q))` for nonnegative `n`. The set $\{N(z) : z \in \mathbb{Z}[\omega]\} = \{0, 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13, 16, 19, 21, 25, 27, 28, \ldots\}$ is the **Loeschian numbers** (OEIS A003136), the integers of the form $a^2 + ab + b^2$. The multiplicative classification states that $n$ is Loeschian iff in its prime factorisation every prime $q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ appears to an even power — the exact analog of the classical sum-of-two-squares classification (every prime $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ appears to even power). Mechanically: (i) `norm_mul` makes the Loeschian set closed under multiplication; (ii) the prime-classification lemma `(p.Prime ∧ p ≠ 3) → (p % 3 = 1 ↔ ∃ z, N(z) = p)` (proved as S5's main theorem in the forward direction, plus a brief modular check for the converse) gives every Loeschian prime; (iii) the splitting/inert/ramified trichotomy `p · ℤ[ω] = 𝔭 · \bar{𝔭}` (split, $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$) vs `p · ℤ[ω] = 𝔭` (inert, $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$) vs `3 · ℤ[ω] = (1 - \omega)^2 · u` (ramified) — derived from the UFD structure once S3 lands — closes the converse via factorisation in the Eisenstein primes. Mathlib bearers: `Nat.factorization`, `Nat.factorization_mul`, `Nat.factorization_pow`, `Nat.Prime`. The downstream payoff: counting Loeschian numbers below $N$ gives $\sim \frac{N}{\sqrt{\log N}}$ (Landau–Ramanujan-type result for the binary quadratic form $a^2 + ab + b^2$), a classical refinement that this formalisation would make machine-checkable.

crossReferences.description: The parent gallery proof formalizes the n = 2 case `p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8) ⟹ p = a² + 2 b²` via `Zsqrtd (-2)`. This file extends to n = 3 via a fresh Eisenstein structure (Zsqrtd does not apply because ℤ[√-3] is non-maximal).
Fermat's two-squares theorem (n = 1 case): `prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⟹ p = a² + b²`. The same proof template extends through n = 2 (parent) and now n = 3 (this file).

Gauss's quadratic reciprocity law supplies the S4 hinge: the splitting argument needs to show $\bigl(\tfrac{-3}{p}\bigr) = 1$ for $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, which reduces by QR to $\bigl(\tfrac{p}{3}\bigr) = 1$, an elementary mod-3 calculation. The Mathlib import `Mathlib.NumberTheory.LegendreSymbol.QuadraticReciprocity` at line 1 is staged forward to provide exactly this equivalence in S4.

The Hurwitz quaternions $\mathcal{H} = \mathbb{Z}\langle 1, i, j, k, (1+i+j+k)/2\rangle$ are the quaternionic analog of the Eisenstein integers: a maximal order strictly larger than $\mathbb{Z}\langle i, j, k\rangle$, with multiplicative norm $N(a+bi+cj+dk) = a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ used to derive Lagrange's four-squares theorem. The same maximal-order phenomenon driving the choice of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ over $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$ here drives the choice of Hurwitz quaternions over Lipschitz quaternions there.

Lagrange's four-squares theorem $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ \exists a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Z},\ n = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2$ uses the **Hurwitz quaternions** $\mathcal{H}$ — a maximal-order construction in the non-commutative algebra $\mathbb{H}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ — exactly as this file uses the **Eisenstein integers** $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ as the maximal order in the commutative algebra $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$. Both proofs share the same three-step skeleton: (i) build a maximal-order ring with a multiplicative norm; (ii) show that any prime factors in that ring (via a left-Euclidean or two-sided Euclidean argument with the norm); (iii) translate the norm equation $p = N(\alpha)$ back to the target quadratic form. The norm-multiplicativity step (`norm_mul` in this file) is the analog of the Euler four-squares identity in the Hurwitz proof.
